summary_plain: This ground-based investigation studied how hot flames transition into cool flames using counterflow configurations and numerical modeling. Researchers examined the conditions affecting flame extinction, flammability limits, and low-temperature chemistry. Understanding these cool and warm flames helps improve spacecraft fire safety by defining potential combustion hazards.
summary_expert: The investigation conducted new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames, building on Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics system. Researchers utilized three numerical modeling schemes: spark-assisted flame propagation of n-heptane/air mixtures, one-dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether flames, and simulated cool flame regimes at elevated pressure up to 20 atm using dimethyl ether/air mixtures. The variables examined included oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes. Results indicated that warm flames feature a double reaction zone structure critical for the transition between cool and hot flames, and that elevated pressures expand the flammable region of warm and cool flames due to increased low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity.

key_findings.text: The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure.
Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications.
